    Publishing MultiplayerHost to NuGet

    Version source

    host/Host.csproj sets the version used for local builds. The publishing workflow uses the pushed Git tag as the release version: v1.5.5 produces package 1.5.5. It passes -p:Version=1.5.5 to build, test, and pack so the assembly and package versions match. No separate version-generation tool is used.

    Choose an unused version and update <Version> in host/Host.csproj to match it. The examples below use 1.5.5 because 1.5.4 has already been published. NuGet package versions are immutable; never move a published release tag or try to replace an existing package with different contents.

    Validate and merge the release

    Use a release branch and a pull request. The protected main branch requires the Build status check before merging.

    From the repository root, restore and build with .NET 11:

    dotnet restore MultiplayerHost_host-only.sln
dotnet build MultiplayerHost_host-only.sln --configuration Release --no-restore

    Run the same test runner used in CI. In PowerShell:

    $env:DOTNET_TEST_RUNNER = 'Microsoft.Testing.Platform'
dotnet test tests/MultiplayerHost.Tests/MultiplayerHost.Tests.csproj --configuration Release --no-build

    In Bash, prefix the test command with DOTNET_TEST_RUNNER=Microsoft.Testing.Platform instead.

    Commit the implementation, tests, documentation, and project version. Push the branch, open a pull request against main, wait for the checks to pass, and merge.

    Tag the merged commit

    With a clean checkout, update local main and tag the merged release commit:

    git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main
git tag -a v1.5.5 -m "MultiplayerHost 1.5.5"
git push origin refs/tags/v1.5.5

    The tag must point to the commit containing the release changes. If main has advanced, pass the intended merged commit SHA to git tag explicitly.

    Automatic NuGet publication

    Pushing a tag matching v*.*.* starts Publish to NuGet. The workflow restores, builds, tests, packs, signs in to NuGet, pushes the package, and archives the .nupkg as a workflow artifact for 30 days.

    Authentication uses NuGet/login@v1 with NuGet user eriba, the GitHub environment publish.yml, and id-token: write. The NuGet trusted-publishing policy must match this repository, .github/workflows/publish.yml, and that environment. It supplies a short-lived API key; no permanent NuGet API key is needed locally.

    Wait for the publish job to succeed, including Push to NuGet. NuGet validation and indexing can delay restore availability after the upload has succeeded. Verify the version on NuGet.org and restore a consumer using NuGet.org and an empty package directory to avoid mistaking a locally packed package for the published release:

    dotnet restore path/to/consumer.csproj --packages ./artifacts/clean-nuget-cache --no-http-cache

    Once verified, update consuming projects to the published version.

    Retrying and troubleshooting

    • For transient workflow failures, rerun the failed job. The push uses --skip-duplicate, so an already published package is not overwritten.
    • Run workflow must target an existing version tag. Dispatching from main fails intentionally because it does not identify a release version.
    • For authentication failures, check the trusted-publishing policy and environment names above. Keep id-token: write enabled.
    • For a successful upload followed by a restore error, wait for NuGet indexing and retry without the HTTP cache. Do not publish different contents under the same version.
    • Fix released code with a new version and a new tag. Workflow-only maintenance applies to future tags; the workflow stored in an existing release tag is unchanged.
